Massachusetts Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: What Owners Should Know

Cash Home Buyers in Massachusetts
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Selling a Massachusetts House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Massachusetts statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Massachusetts law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Massachusetts courts quote that a claimant must show 'actual, open, exclusive, and adverse possession'; failure to establish any element is fatal. The Mass.gov law-library page lists the elements as continuous, exclusive, hostile, open, and notorious. (Massachusetts law about adverse possession (Mass.gov, Trial Court Law Libraries); source)
  • No title to registered land can be acquired through adverse possession. (M.G.L. c. 185, § 53 (cited on Mass.gov adverse possession page); source)
Selling in Massachusetts?
We buy Massachusetts houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Details we could not confirm on an official page are not stated here. Read the statute sections linked above for the full text, and confirm deadlines with the court or county office.

How to sell a Massachusetts house when this applies to you

  1. Write down who is in the house and on what terms: owner, heirs, tenants or occupants with no lease.
  2. Ask the title company what it needs to insure the sale, such as a recorded deed, court papers or a payoff letter.
  3. Get the payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the proceeds at closing.
  4. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. See we buy houses in Massachusetts.

What a cash sale of a Massachusetts house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Massachusetts.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Massachusetts disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Massachusetts

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Massachusetts change, so confirm details with the official office or a Massachusetts attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Massachusetts

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Massachusetts Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Massachusetts house?

Only by meeting every requirement of the adverse possession statute cited above for the full period. Check the statute and talk to a Massachusetts attorney about your facts.

Can I sell a house that has squatters in it?

Yes. We buy houses as-is, including occupied ones. Tell us who is in the property when you request an offer.

Should I remove a squatter myself?

No. Use the legal process described in the official sources above. Self-help removal can create liability for the owner.

Massachusetts Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Massachusetts statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Massachusetts statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • At or before tenancy start a landlord may not require more than first month's rent, last month's rent at the same rate, and a security deposit equal to the first month's rent. (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B(1)(b); source)
  • If the landlord fails to comply with certain deposit duties, the tenant is awarded three times the deposit plus 5% interest from when payment was due, plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Tenant must get a receipt at the time of the deposit and, within 30 days, a receipt naming the bank and account. (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B(3)(b), (7); source)
  • Where rent is paid monthly in a tenancy at will, either party may end it with notice of 30 days or one month before the next rent due date, whichever is longer; rent can change with notice on the same terms. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • Landlord must arrange with the tenant in advance to enter to repair, inspect or show the unit; entry without approval is allowed only for an emergency with potential to damage the whole building, or apparent abandonment. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • Landlord must provide a unit compliant with the Massachusetts State Sanitary Code (105 CMR 410) and maintain it in habitable condition throughout the tenancy. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • Certain landlord conduct within six months of a tenant's protected activity (e.g., reporting Sanitary Code violations) is presumed retaliatory. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • No lease may impose interest or a penalty for late rent until 30 days after the rent is due. (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B(1)(c); source)

Massachusetts law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A notice to quit gives 14 days (nonpayment) or 30 days (other reasons) before the landlord may go to court; a notice to quit is required before filing summary process. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
  • Landlords can file in a District Court or Housing Court. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
  • Tenant has 10 days from entry of judgment to appeal; the landlord can hire a sheriff or constable 11 days after the final decision; the officer must give written notice 2 days (excluding weekends/holidays) before removal; removals only Monday-Friday 9 a.m.-5 p.m. and the execution must be used within 3 months. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
  • Officer removes tenant's belongings to a licensed storage facility; tenant may owe storage fees. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
